VII. What the Imam Means in Shiite Spiritual Life
passage-en-01813

The line of Imams therefore continues, whether openly or in concealment, in order to preserve the Prophet's spiritual inheritance—not to maintain any particular political order. In fact, apart from the First Imam, none of the Twelve exercised earthly political authority. Yet each was fully an Imam. This is central to Shiism and shapes its understanding of Islam.
VII. What the Imam Means in Shiite Spiritual Life
passage-en-01814

We have been told that the Prophet and the Imam do not exist merely because human beings need them to manage their religious and worldly affairs. Of course, the proper conduct of those affairs presupposes their existence.
VII. What the Imam Means in Shiite Spiritual Life
passage-en-01815

But the Earth continues to exist through the Imam for a deeper, spiritual reason: his level of being is that of the Perfect Human Being. Because the Perfect Human Being is the purpose and ultimate goal (ghayat, telos) of the earthly world, the human world could not even continue to exist without him.
VII. What the Imam Means in Shiite Spiritual Life
passage-en-01816

This is precisely the meaning of the mysterious existence of the Twelfth Imam, “hidden from the senses but present in the hearts of his followers.” He is the spiritual Pole of existence, and that is what he remains. His Imamate does not depend on anyone recognising him. As we have said, the line of Imams is not just another dynasty among other dynasties. An Imam is not a claimant to the Imamate. He is the Imam. “We are like the Israelites among Pharaoh's people,” declared the Fourth Imam. The line of Imams has withdrawn into concealment, like the last guardian of the Grail.
VII. What the Imam Means in Shiite Spiritual Life
passage-en-01817

Yet through this line there continues, without interruption until the Last Day, the silsilat al-irfan: the living succession of spiritual knowledge that the First Imam taught his disciple Komayl ibn Ziyad. The spiritual centre of this succession is the Twelfth Imam, the Imam now in concealment. Those who belong to it recognise and are recognised by the people who call themselves the people of the A'raf. This gives the Imam's role in Shiite spirituality an even deeper meaning: he guides us towards knowledge of ourselves.
VII. What the Imam Means in Shiite Spiritual Life
en-book-1-ch-7-s3
3. The Imam as the A'raf
VII. What the Imam Means in Shiite Spiritual Life
passage-en-01818

The A'raf is the mysterious barrier mentioned in the Qur'an between Paradise and Hell. The seventh sura takes its name from it. In verses 44–45, we read: “On the A'raf stand people who recognise each person by their appearance” (7:44). A disciple relates an answer given by the Sixth Imam, who repeats a saying of the First Imam, when someone asks about the people of the A'raf:
VII. What the Imam Means in Shiite Spiritual Life
passage-en-01819

“It is we [the Imams] who stand upon the A'raf. We recognise our companions by their faces. And we ourselves are the A'raf, because God can be known only through knowing us. We are the A'raf because, on the Day of Resurrection, God knows us as the Way (sirat). No one enters Paradise except those who know us and whom we know. No one enters the Fire except those who deny us and whom we deny.
VII. What the Imam Means in Shiite Spiritual Life
passage-en-01820

“Had God Most High wished, He could have made Himself known to humanity directly. Instead, He made us His thresholds, His way, His path, the Face towards which people must turn. Whoever turns away from our walayat—refusing us the devotion of love—or prefers others to us, turns away from the Way.”
VII. What the Imam Means in Shiite Spiritual Life
passage-en-01821

The Imam's answer moves through three stages, until the Imam and the A'raf are identified with one another. Mulla Sadra begins by showing how commentators concerned only with the outward meaning of scripture have largely missed the point. Even interpreters outside Shiism who seek hidden meanings have failed to grasp what is essential about the A'raf. He therefore follows the Imam's words one phrase at a time, looking for an interpretation rooted in the Imams' own teaching. The name A'raf comes from the Arabic root 'rf, associated with knowing and recognising. Once we understand that connection, we can follow the three steps in the Imam's answer.
VII. What the Imam Means in Shiite Spiritual Life
passage-en-01822

1. At the first level, the Imam says: “It is we [the Twelve Imams] who stand upon the A'raf.” This means that they stand at the summit of knowledge (ma'rifat), its highest point. The height is spiritual, not a location somewhere in physical space.
VII. What the Imam Means in Shiite Spiritual Life
passage-en-01823

2. At the second level, something remarkable happens. The Imam no longer says simply that the Imams stand upon the A'raf; he says that they are the A'raf itself. In other words, all human knowledge of God passes through knowing them. They are not merely people who know, whose knowledge stands at the summit of all knowledge. They are also what makes this knowledge possible. They are the very reality reached by the highest knowledge—its object as well as its source.
VII. What the Imam Means in Shiite Spiritual Life
passage-en-01824

Here a person's name, or the quality that defines that person, is used to name the thing itself: in this case, knowledge, of which the Imams are the source. At the first level of the answer, A'raf refers to knowledge or direct spiritual understanding (ma'rifat). “We stand at the summit of the A'raf” means: we stand at the highest point of that understanding.
VII. What the Imam Means in Shiite Spiritual Life
passage-en-01825

At the second level, A'raf names the cause of this knowledge, the reality that makes it possible. “We are the A'raf” means: through us, human beings are able to know God. We are what human knowledge of God reaches, because we are the form in which God becomes manifest—a theophany.
VII. What the Imam Means in Shiite Spiritual Life
passage-en-01826

To put it another way, knowledge of God (ma'rifat Allah) is possible only for the person who knows the Imams. We have already seen that the Imam is the form in which God reveals Himself. The Imam is the “Face” through which God is known, the form God necessarily takes in any human knowledge or experience of Him. Without that Face, God remains entirely hidden, the Absconditum. As the A'raf, the Imam is this supreme Face: the one through whom human knowledge of God becomes possible.
VII. What the Imam Means in Shiite Spiritual Life
passage-en-01827

We recognise here the meaning of the Imam for Shiite spiritual life that we examined earlier. The Imams themselves teach the connection between two sayings. An Imam can say, “Whoever knows us knows their Lord.” And the spiritual teachers repeatedly say, “Whoever knows themselves—their own soul—knows their Lord.” The two sayings belong together because, in knowing one's deepest self, or soul (anima), one comes to know one's Imam. And whoever knows their Imam knows their Lord.
VII. What the Imam Means in Shiite Spiritual Life
passage-en-01828
Thus the ideas of the Imam and the deepest Self meet: to know one's Imam is to know oneself; to know oneself is to know one's Imam—the Soul of one's soul—and therefore to know one's Lord.
VII. What the Imam Means in Shiite Spiritual Life
passage-en-01829

What Shiite spirituality offers through the persons of the Twelve Imams, through their “forms of light,” is access to this self-knowledge without which there can be no knowledge of God. It is an awareness of the personal relationship through which God is present as this particular God, appearing in this particular way, to the person who worships Him.
VII. What the Imam Means in Shiite Spiritual Life
passage-en-01830

This explains the importance of dreams in which the Imams appear. A believer who receives such a vision discovers their most intimate secret: the Imam as the Soul of their soul, the hidden meaning of their own knowledge of God. Earlier we spoke about the human meaning of knowing God. Now the Imam also reveals the divine meaning of this human knowledge.
VII. What the Imam Means in Shiite Spiritual Life
passage-en-01831

3. At the third level, the Imam goes further still: “We are the A'raf because, on the Day of Resurrection, God knows us as the Way.” Here A'raf refers to what is known in its own essential nature, not to something known incidentally or from the outside.
VII. What the Imam Means in Shiite Spiritual Life
passage-en-01832
What does this essential knowledge mean? At the second level, the Imam was the knowledge through which a person knows God. At the third, he is the divine knowledge through which God knows a person.
VII. What the Imam Means in Shiite Spiritual Life
passage-en-01833
The Imam says that God knows someone who knows the Imams as a person of Paradise.
VII. What the Imam Means in Shiite Spiritual Life
passage-en-01834

The second level tells us that a believer's knowledge of the Imams is their knowledge of God. The third tells us that God's knowledge of the believer is the believer's knowledge of the Imams. By knowing the Imams, a person knows themselves as someone belonging to Paradise, and this is also God's knowledge of them. Conversely, the person who rejects the Imams has a sense of self that is itself their hell.
VII. What the Imam Means in Shiite Spiritual Life
passage-en-01835

“No one enters the Fire except those who deny us and whom we deny.” That denial is also the way God knows the person who rejects the Imams. It is the one who denies who drives God out of their own paradise; that is what hell means here. At the point where knowing the Imam and knowing oneself become one, the outward image of the A'raf as a barrier reveals its full meaning: the Imam truly is the boundary separating Paradise from Hell.
VII. What the Imam Means in Shiite Spiritual Life
passage-en-01836

This teaching offers the philosopher endless possibilities for reflection. The Imam is the knowledge a human being has of God, and for that very reason he is also the knowledge God has of a human being. The two statements place the Imam at the level of the first manifestation of God, at the very dawn of God's becoming knowable.
VII. What the Imam Means in Shiite Spiritual Life
passage-en-01837

We have already witnessed the rising of this dawn in other texts (above, pp. 296–297). There, a particular divine will emerged on the horizon of a universal, primordial Will. That dawn made possible the appearance of a form (tajalli) in which God could become the object of love—His mahbubiya, or being loved.
VII. What the Imam Means in Shiite Spiritual Life
passage-en-01838

In that earlier account, the emphasis on divine will went with a view of existence found in a Shaykhi master such as Muhammad Karim Khan Kirmani. He refuses to include God's ineffable, indescribable Being within a single, unqualified unity of being (wahdat al-wujud). Here, with Mulla Sadra Shirazi, we encounter a thinker who accepts that unity. His account of reality begins instead with knowledge.
VII. What the Imam Means in Shiite Spiritual Life
passage-en-01839

There is, first, an all-encompassing divine knowledge: perfect knowledge identical with the simple, undivided essence of God. It contains no multiplicity, because the divine Essence (dhat) is the source from which the existence of everything flows. When God knows Himself, He knows all things through the very act of knowing that is identical with His Essence. There is also God's knowledge of individual things. This can mean that the essences of things are present to Him as they exist concretely, or that their Ideas are made real in being “before” they exist in the concrete world.
VII. What the Imam Means in Shiite Spiritual Life
passage-en-01840

Together these levels form an order of causes and effects. Mulla Sadra explains that its downward and upward movements mirror one another exactly. In the downward movement, angels act as causes that gradually bring creatures' potential existence into reality. In the upward movement, prophets, Imams and all God's Friends serve as causes and guides who awaken the potential angelic nature within human beings. They lift people beyond the merely animal level and bring their angelic possibilities into full reality, so that they become people of Paradise (ahl al-jinnat).
VII. What the Imam Means in Shiite Spiritual Life
passage-en-01841

The same pattern applies to divine knowledge. In the order of creation, God knows the beings of this changing world through His knowledge of their angels—the intellectual and heavenly angels described in the philosophical system of Avicenna. That is why angels are called the “witnesses” (shuhada) of creation before God. In the order of the last things, God knows the faithfulness of believers through His knowledge of the prophets and God's Friends. They, in turn, are God's witnesses for humanity on the Day of Resurrection.
VII. What the Imam Means in Shiite Spiritual Life
passage-en-01842

Through this idea of the witnesses, the Imam's words lead the philosopher to see the parallel between the role of angels in the origin and ordering of the world—the order of the mabda', or Beginning—and the role of the Imams in the return of souls to their source—the order of the ma'ad, or Return.
VII. What the Imam Means in Shiite Spiritual Life
passage-en-01843

The second concerns salvation and what awaits us at the end of earthly life. Both the teaching about angels and the teaching about the Imams have their deepest foundation in divine knowledge. Both reach their highest expression in the idea of the Witness.
VII. What the Imam Means in Shiite Spiritual Life
passage-en-01844

In that idea, a philosophy of presence and a spiritual experience of presence come together. Everything in prophetic philosophy points towards it. The Imam is the meeting point where the Witness, the one who beholds (shahid)—the Imam standing upon the A'raf—is also the one beheld (mashhud), the Witness who is himself present to contemplation: the A'raf itself. He bears witness to the God he contemplates, speaking for God before humanity.
VII. What the Imam Means in Shiite Spiritual Life
passage-en-01845

Yet he is also the one human beings behold when God reveals Himself to them. He is the eye through which God looks towards humanity and cares for it, because he is also the eye through which humanity looks towards God and turns towards Him.
VII. What the Imam Means in Shiite Spiritual Life
passage-en-01846
We shall see this theme develop in Ruzbihan's mysticism (Book Three below).
VII. What the Imam Means in Shiite Spiritual Life
passage-en-01847

The Imams are both the eyes through which God looks upon this world and the eyes through which human beings contemplate the divine attributes, since God's Essence itself is beyond their reach. The Imam is thus at once the one who contemplates and the one contemplated (shahid–mashhud), beheld by God and by humanity. He keeps us from both extremes: denying any meaningful manifestation of God's attributes (ta'til), and making God resemble created beings (tashbih). My knowledge of the Imam is therefore also God's knowledge of me. This is why the Imam is the barrier that separates the people of Paradise from the people of Hell.
VII. What the Imam Means in Shiite Spiritual Life
passage-en-01848

As Mulla Sadra puts it: “God's knowledge of the spiritual condition of these two groups passes through His knowledge of the Witnesses in their twofold role: bearing witness to the Paradise of some and the Hell of others. This is the deeper understanding (tahqiq) of the prophets and Imams as God's Witnesses before humanity, and of the Qur'anic verse: ‘What will happen when We bring forth a witness from every community, and bring you forth as a witness against these people?’ (4:45).”
VII. What the Imam Means in Shiite Spiritual Life
passage-en-01849

Now the full meaning of the Imam's three successive statements becomes clear. “We are the A'raf” means: in our very essence, we are those whom God knows (ma'rufun bi'l-dhat), those whom He contemplates (mashhudun li'llah), His direct witnesses in contemplation. We do not need intermediaries, because we ourselves serve as intermediaries for others. We are the highest stages of the Way (sirat) through which human beings must pass to reach the greatest possible closeness to God.
VII. What the Imam Means in Shiite Spiritual Life
passage-en-01850

The A'raf thus emerges as the summit, the protective boundary, of the philosophy of prophecy and the Imams. That philosophy offers the gift of the highest wisdom. The Imam Ja'far explains this to a disciple while commenting on a Qur'anic verse (2:272): “Whoever has been given wisdom has received an immense good” (compare Proverbs 3:13 and following). “This wisdom (hikmat),” he says, “is spiritual awareness, the direct knowledge (ma'rifat) of the Imam.”
VII. What the Imam Means in Shiite Spiritual Life
passage-en-01851

Several ideas prepare us to understand what this wisdom means. The most important is that of the Hojjat, to which Sadra Shirazi returns repeatedly in his commentary on the Imams' sayings. There are two kinds of Hojjat: two kinds of witness, guide and guarantor. The first is the outer guide: the prophet who brings God's message to humanity, and, after the Prophet, the Imams for those who need a guide they can see.
VII. What the Imam Means in Shiite Spiritual Life
passage-en-01852
But Twelver Shiism, living under the guidance of the Hidden Imam, naturally leads us towards the second: the invisible inner guide, the Imam within (Hojjat batina, Imam dakhili).
VII. What the Imam Means in Shiite Spiritual Life
passage-en-01853

This inner guide is a radiant, holy light. It comes from the divine Throne and rises at the eastern horizon of the soul, at its highest point. It illuminates the “senses of the heart,” through which the prophetic message can be heard in its hidden meaning: the walayat of the Imams. It is a secret, inward prophecy (nobowwat batiniya) concerned with unseen worlds and the hidden life of the soul.
VII. What the Imam Means in Shiite Spiritual Life
passage-en-01854

The idea of an inner guide does not make the teachings about prophecy or the Imams unnecessary. Quite the opposite: it brings them to fulfilment. This is where the teaching of the Imams is meant to lead. The inner guide reached through this process protects the mystic from the intoxication of a spiritual pride that would make them imagine themselves godlike.
VII. What the Imam Means in Shiite Spiritual Life
passage-en-01855

Before entering the Way, the mystic is still the person addressed by the Fifth Imam's warning: “You know even less about the roads of Heaven than you do about the roads of Earth.” The Shiite believer's “search for the Imam” is therefore not a search for someone familiar with the physical spaces of the astronomical sky. It concerns another world entirely, one that “corresponds to inward, invisible forms, which cannot be perceived by our physical senses, but only by our spiritual senses.”
VII. What the Imam Means in Shiite Spiritual Life
passage-en-01856

So when the Imam speaks of wisdom, with its successive levels expressed as faith in God, His angels, His revealed books, His messengers and the Resurrection, Sadra reminds us that wisdom is twofold, just as the Hojjat or guide is twofold. There is revealed wisdom (hikmat makshufa) and veiled wisdom (hikmat mastura). Revealed wisdom is embodied in the visible persons of the sages: they are wisdom made present as living human beings.
VII. What the Imam Means in Shiite Spiritual Life
passage-en-01857

Whoever sees one of them with the “eyes of the heart,” which reveal the sage's true nature, sees wisdom in personal form. For ordinary people, this is God's gift of wisdom, the “immense good” spoken of in the sacred text: the visible person of the Imam, who is wisdom itself (nafs al-hikmat).
VII. What the Imam Means in Shiite Spiritual Life
passage-en-01858

Veiled wisdom, by contrast, is the wisdom within the hearts of God's Friends (awliya), the prophets and the Imams—the hukama ilahiyun, sages of God, or “theosophers” in the full original sense of lovers of divine wisdom. The Imams' teaching about the A'raf helps us understand why each Imam is a sage from one point of view, and wisdom itself from another.
VII. What the Imam Means in Shiite Spiritual Life
passage-en-01859

A deep joy runs through Mulla Sadra's reflections at this point. He reaches the place where Shiite spirituality meets his own philosophy of being and knowledge, shaped by the tradition of illumination. Both come together in the spiritual awareness of the Shiite philosopher devoted to that tradition.
VII. What the Imam Means in Shiite Spiritual Life
passage-en-01860

The union of the sage and wisdom, he tells us, is like what happens in the act of understanding: the person who understands ('aqil) and the intelligence actually at work ('aql) become one. This expresses the distinctive character of this form of Shiite spirituality, which we have already encountered: philosophical thought and spiritual fulfilment cannot be separated from one another. Each depends on the other (see also Book Two, on Suhrawardi, and Book Five).
VII. What the Imam Means in Shiite Spiritual Life
passage-en-01861

The twofold Hojjat and the twofold wisdom are really two ways of describing the same thing. In the Imam, there is a wisdom made visible and a wisdom that remains hidden (makhfiya). The visible wisdom is the Imam's person, present before our eyes. The hidden wisdom is an inward light of spirit and understanding (nur batini 'aqli). This light is the Imam's spiritual life. Through it, the person he guides is able to see the world beyond death, together with the heavenly beings and forms within it. That illumination is the gift of wisdom.
VII. What the Imam Means in Shiite Spiritual Life
passage-en-01862

When someone truly understands, the act of intelligence is not something added to them from outside. Their understanding is part of what they are at that moment. In the same way, the sage—the Imam—is wisdom itself. To know this sage through direct spiritual knowledge (ma'rifat) is to know the wisdom that he embodies.
VII. What the Imam Means in Shiite Spiritual Life
passage-en-01863
But in that very act of knowing, the Imam's wisdom becomes the wisdom of the believer who follows him, just as intelligence becomes the living activity of the person who understands.
VII. What the Imam Means in Shiite Spiritual Life
passage-en-01864

The believer then discovers that two sayings express the same truth from opposite sides: “Whoever knows their Imam knows their Lord,” and “Whoever knows themselves knows their Lord”—which here also means knowing their Imam. To be fully aware of one's Imam, one's personal and invisible inner guide, is to become someone in whom the wisdom embodied by the Imam has come to life. Such a person possesses the “inner Witness,” who is precisely the Imam himself as the Imam within (Imam dakhili), the “divine Face” that remains when everything else passes away.
VII. What the Imam Means in Shiite Spiritual Life
passage-en-01865

We said earlier that the Imam is the form in which God appears. In the same way, the faithful believer becomes the form in which the Imam appears. This is the heart of spirituality centred on the Imams: the outer Imam leads us to the inner Imam, and knowing the Imam leads us to knowledge of ourselves.
VII. What the Imam Means in Shiite Spiritual Life
passage-en-01866

We can now reflect on what each of the Shiite Imams, and all twelve together in their spiritual fullness, mean for Shiite life. The teaching of the A'raf reaches its highest point in a philosophy of the Witness (shahid) and of the presence experienced through witnessing (shuhud).
VII. What the Imam Means in Shiite Spiritual Life
passage-en-01867

The Imam becomes, in a sense, the active awareness of the believer. This is how the silsilat al-irfan, the succession of spiritual knowledge, continues in the world. It is unknown to most people: the hidden line of those who play their part in the sacred history of the age of walayat, and who are truly “alive” in the fullest sense of that word.
VII. What the Imam Means in Shiite Spiritual Life
passage-en-01868

This “community of the living” extends towards a shared spiritual faith that reaches across the whole history of prophecy. Its foundation is the same understanding of the inner meaning of religion. Earlier (§ 1), the idea of universal walayat, of which the Imam is the Seal, already brought us to this point. All the prophets of earlier ages, together with their believers, belong to the same eternal prophetic religion. Together they form a single spiritual body (corpus mysticum), the “Temple of Light” of the Imamate, as Ismaili writers call it.
VII. What the Imam Means in Shiite Spiritual Life
passage-en-01869

Mulla Sadra writes: “This has been true in every age, and it will remain true in the future. All the sages of God ('ulama rabbaniyun, the theosophoi), all the prophets and all their Imams, together belong to one religion (din wahid) and one school (madhhab wahid). Or, better still, they form something like one complete spiritual person (shakhs wahid kulli 'aqli). In the same way, the believers who follow them, wherever and whenever they live, are like a single Soul. The school of every Imam is also the school of every other Imam, and at the same time the school of all the prophets and God's Friends.”
VII. What the Imam Means in Shiite Spiritual Life
passage-en-01870
These words of Mulla Sadra could stand as the declaration of faith of Shiite inner spirituality: faith in an eternal Ecclesia spiritualis, a community joined together in spirit.
VII. What the Imam Means in Shiite Spiritual Life
en-book-1-ch-7-s4
4. The Imam as God's Witness and the Witness of Contemplation
VII. What the Imam Means in Shiite Spiritual Life
passage-en-01871

The texts we have examined and discussed have, I believe, told us what matters most. Yet Mulla Sadra's final pages on Kolayni's Kafi—the pages he still had time to write before his death—add a number of illuminating refinements.
VII. What the Imam Means in Shiite Spiritual Life
passage-en-01872

Sadly, they break off in full flight, with the same poignant abruptness as Bach's unfinished Art of Fugue. They end just as we are about to discover the Shiite thinker's deepest meditation on one of the high points of the Imams' own teaching about the Imam, a text he was explaining line by line. Here I can offer only a brief outline and paraphrase of these extraordinarily dense final pages.
VII. What the Imam Means in Shiite Spiritual Life
passage-en-01873

The whole commentary on the Twelve Imams as the “Witnesses of God” (shohadâ' Allah) is guided by a single insight: the degree to which something exists—its very act of being (wojûd)—depends on, and is proportional to, its degree of presence (hodûr, hozûr). And presence is essential to what it means to be a witness (shâhid). Here Mulla Sadra's entire metaphysics of being rests upon the understanding of the Imam and is bound to its central theme.
VII. What the Imam Means in Shiite Spiritual Life
passage-en-01874

Sadra begins with an extended discussion of two words, shâhid and shahîd (distinguished in our transliteration by the position of the circumflex). Shâhid, the one who witnesses, is the active form of shohûd—being present to something, witnessing it directly, seeing it with one's own eyes—and is related to moshâhadat, vision or contemplation. In mystical language, this means the visionary perception of worlds that the mystic beholds but that remain invisible to others.
VII. What the Imam Means in Shiite Spiritual Life
passage-en-01875

All of this presupposes that one being can be present to another. The shâhid, the witness who contemplates something, is the one to whom, and within whom, the form or image of that thing is present. The shahîd, by contrast, is the Witnessing One—the “martyr” in the word's original sense of someone who bears witness. It is the faculty or power (qowwat) through which the witness's vision (shohûd) and presence (hodûr) become possible.
VII. What the Imam Means in Shiite Spiritual Life
passage-en-01876

What, then, makes it possible for one being to be present to another—the very condition of witnessing? Many things, by their fundamental nature, cannot receive the presence of another thing or themselves become present to it. This is true of all material things situated in the perceptible space of our darkened world. None can be inwardly present to another, or present for another; and no other thing can be present in or for it.
VII. What the Imam Means in Shiite Spiritual Life
passage-en-01877

We cannot say, for example, that the Earth, as a physical mass, exists as a “presence” for the starry heavens, or the reverse; nor that the element air is present to the element water, or the reverse. That is why this world is the dwelling place of unconsciousness and death.
VII. What the Imam Means in Shiite Spiritual Life
passage-en-01878

Everything is immersed in darkness and unconsciousness to the degree that it belongs to this world and is remote from the world of Light, Knowledge, and Life—the world beyond, the dwelling place of the Living. Conversely, consciousness and presence grow in proportion to the light received from the Malakut, the spiritual world.
VII. What the Imam Means in Shiite Spiritual Life
passage-en-01879
When Mulla Sadra says that the degree of existence is proportional to the degree of presence, his insight comes close to one expressed in language familiar today.
VII. What the Imam Means in Shiite Spiritual Life
passage-en-01880

But we must be careful. For Sadra and the Ishrâqîyûn, the philosophers of illumination, this is a way of being in the present world fundamentally different from an existence irretrievably cast into it, abandoned to its “being-toward-death.” What the relation between existence and presence means for Sadra is this: the more intense one's presence becomes, the more one is present to other worlds—and the more one escapes the conditions of unconsciousness, death, and absence.
VII. What the Imam Means in Shiite Spiritual Life
passage-en-01881

The more fully a human life becomes Presence, the more that person witnesses other worlds. Such a life becomes less a being-toward-death and more a being-toward-what-lies-beyond-death. A metaphysics of Presence thus unfolds into a metaphysics of vision, of the presence through which one witnesses (shohûd). This has already been announced in the teaching about the Imam and is realized as that teaching becomes an inner experience (above, § 3).
VII. What the Imam Means in Shiite Spiritual Life
passage-en-01882

Presence must therefore have degrees of intensity. These are marked by stages of becoming immaterial (tajarrod) and correspond to different levels of perception and awareness: sensory perception, imaginative perception, and intellectual understanding. At every level, the principle of unity described earlier applies.
VII. What the Imam Means in Shiite Spiritual Life
passage-en-01883

What we perceive through the senses, imagine, or understand is not the external material thing itself, but its form—sensory, imaginal, or intellectual—as it is present within us. An understood form is such a form only in relation to someone who understands it. The act of understanding is not something added to the person who understands: it is that person in the very act of understanding. The same holds for sensory and imaginal forms.
VII. What the Imam Means in Shiite Spiritual Life
passage-en-01884

Thus, the form understood (ma'qûla) itself becomes, precisely as understood, an understanding form, an active form. The same is true of sensory and imaginal forms. Seen in this light, knowing proves to be the very source of spiritual life. This is the spiritual meaning of “oriental presence” (hozûr ishrâqî): presence is called oriental because it rises at the East of the soul, when the soul itself becomes the East, the dawning place, of its own knowing.
VII. What the Imam Means in Shiite Spiritual Life
passage-en-01885

Here too lies the whole metaphysics of Witness and Witnessing. My spiritual awareness (ma'rifat) of the Imam brings about the Imam's presence within me. The Imam then becomes the “inner Imam,” the Witnessing One, the active consciousness present within me (shahîd). This is why we can say that every prophet, and every Imam after him, serves as the very faculty of knowing in each of his followers.
VII. What the Imam Means in Shiite Spiritual Life
passage-en-01886

For the follower, precisely as a follower, can have neither knowledge ('ilm) nor testimony (shahâdat)—can neither be “present to” nor have something “present within”—except through the knowledge and testimony of the Imam. He becomes, as we said earlier, “the eye through which he sees.”
VII. What the Imam Means in Shiite Spiritual Life
passage-en-01887
Let us draw the threads together. The Imam is God's Witness (shâhid).
VII. What the Imam Means in Shiite Spiritual Life
passage-en-01888

But what does he witness? In discussing the A'râf, we encountered this declaration by an Imam: “We are what God knows; we are the essential object of divine knowledge.” The Imam as shâhid, the one who contemplates, is at the same time the mashhûd, the one contemplated: the object of God's contemplation and therefore the form and content of divine knowledge—the form in which that knowledge becomes known to us as human beings.
VII. What the Imam Means in Shiite Spiritual Life
passage-en-01889

And if the Imam is the Witness of God for his follower, the form through which that follower knows God, then the Imam must at the same time be the one whom the follower contemplates, his mashhûd. He is Witness and Witnessed, Contemplator and Contemplated (shâhid-mashhûd): the Witness whom one contemplates, the Witness of contemplation.
VII. What the Imam Means in Shiite Spiritual Life
passage-en-01890

In contemplating this Witness, the follower contemplates the very one whom God contemplates—the object of divine knowledge and contemplation—which the follower can contemplate nowhere except in this Witness. The act of contemplation makes the Witness present within the follower. This mystery of shared presence, of two beings present to one another, is what we mean by the Imam as the inner Witness (Hojjat bâtina). What the follower beholds and attests is what this Witness himself beholds and attests.
VII. What the Imam Means in Shiite Spiritual Life
passage-en-01891

Indeed, the follower can see and contemplate it only by contemplating the Witness, because the Witness is necessarily the form in which the follower can know the God to whom the Witness bears testimony. Such knowledge means that the Witness is present within the follower; at the same time, it means that the follower is present to the Witness. And to be present to this Witness is already to be present to the One to whom he bears witness.
VII. What the Imam Means in Shiite Spiritual Life
passage-en-01892

As we have said, the follower's knowledge of this Witness is therefore, in that very act, God's knowledge of the follower: God knows the follower in the one who bears witness to that follower before Him. The Imam is the Witness whom God beholds, through whom God is beheld, and through whom God beholds. It is through this inner Imam, the “Imam of one's own being,” that God knows the follower. “We are the essential object of divine knowledge,” said the Imam.
VII. What the Imam Means in Shiite Spiritual Life
passage-en-01893

What God knows in this Witness is therefore every person to whom that Witness is present and who is present to him. We have already seen Mulla Sadra draw a fundamental parallel. Just as God knows the beings brought forth in the creation of the cosmos through their Angels, so He knows those making their Return to Him through the Imams and the Awliyâ, the friends of God.
VII. What the Imam Means in Shiite Spiritual Life
passage-en-01894

Since the Imam is the essential object of divine knowledge, to know the Imam is, in that very act, to know God's knowledge of His follower. Once again we return to the saying we have repeated so often, because its meaning can never be exhausted: “Whoever knows himself knows his Lord.”
VII. What the Imam Means in Shiite Spiritual Life
passage-en-01895

To know oneself—to know the Soul of one's soul—is to know one's Imam. And the Imam is precisely the object of divine knowledge: what God knows of the human being and within the human being. The follower's presence to God and God's answering presence to the follower—this is the Imam, the mutual presence established without either ta'tîl (denying God's attributes) or tashbîh (making God resemble His creatures).
VII. What the Imam Means in Shiite Spiritual Life
passage-en-01896

The ishrâqî or “oriental” metaphysics of illumination thus reaches its summit in a metaphysics of the Imamate. At its heart stands a Shiite spiritual life centered on the Imam: God present to the Imam who is present to the human being; God present to the human being who is present to the Imam; the Imam present to the human being who is present to himself.
VII. What the Imam Means in Shiite Spiritual Life
passage-en-01897

Through a similar deepening of spiritual understanding, we shall see Semnani use his interpretation of sacred texts to discover the “prophets of your being” (below, Book IV, Chapter IV). For the Sufi master Ruzbihan of Shiraz, every beautiful face—because its beauty testifies that its Creator is present to that beauty—becomes the shâhid-mashhûd, the Contemplator-Contemplated, the Witness of contemplation (below, Book III).
VII. What the Imam Means in Shiite Spiritual Life
passage-en-01898

But we may ask whether this disclosure of the divine “Face” in a human face would have been possible, even in Sufism outside Shiism, without the mediation of Shiite teaching about the Imam: without the revelation of God's “Face” in the heavenly Anthropos, the luminous Forms of the Fourteen Immaculate Ones.
VII. What the Imam Means in Shiite Spiritual Life
passage-en-01899

This mediation is indeed proclaimed in the Quranic verse: “We have made you a mediating community” (2:137). Imam Ja'far explains this verse at length to a disciple. The community occupying this middle or mediating position is not the Arabs, as some interpretations concerned only with the outward meaning would have it.
VII. What the Imam Means in Shiite Spiritual Life
passage-en-01900

No: it is the Imams. They mediate between two acts of testimony: they are witnesses for humanity, while the Prophet is a witness for them. As their initiator, the Prophet acts as their active faculty of knowledge and vision, just as each Imam does for his follower.
VII. What the Imam Means in Shiite Spiritual Life
passage-en-01901

We now come to the last description of the Imams that Mulla Sadra had time to examine before leaving this world. Just as the sage is also wisdom, and the one who contemplates is also the one contemplated, so the Keeper of the treasure of divine knowledge is the Treasure itself.
VII. What the Imam Means in Shiite Spiritual Life
passage-en-01902

A disciple relates: “I heard Imam Ja'far declare: We are the guardians of the res divina (amr ilâhî, the divine affair), the Keepers of the treasure of divine knowledge, the Watchers over the secret of divine Revelation.” When the Imam says “we are the guardians,” he uses the word hâfiz.
VII. What the Imam Means in Shiite Spiritual Life
passage-en-01903

Philosophers, meanwhile, give this name to the “faculty that preserves” (qowwat hâfiza) the forms of knowledge—the faculty that serves as their storehouse or treasure. They say that imagination is the treasury preserving the forms of sensory perception, while the Active Intelligence is the treasury of things understood by the intellect.
VII. What the Imam Means in Shiite Spiritual Life
passage-en-01904

From here Mulla Sadra's meditation takes flight, but we cannot follow it to its destination: that destination would have appeared in the unfinished portion of his commentary. Even so, we can clearly discern the summit toward which his understanding of the Imam was leading.
VII. What the Imam Means in Shiite Spiritual Life
passage-en-01905

On the one hand, the Treasures of divine knowledge can only be intellectual Essences, beings of light, free from any mixture with material substance and fully actual in their knowledge and understanding. They cannot, therefore, be forms impressed upon bodies, or even souls, since a soul still possesses only the potential for perfect intellectual understanding.
VII. What the Imam Means in Shiite Spiritual Life
passage-en-01906

Mulla Sadra writes: “It is therefore established that there exist spiritual beings, intellectual Essences, in whom all existing things are fully actual in a spiritual and intellectual way. Through them souls are brought to perfection and become beings who understand in actuality, having formerly been receptive beings capable of understanding only in potential. These spiritual beings stand between God and humanity as intermediaries through whom spiritual blessings and influences are continually bestowed and descend.
VII. What the Imam Means in Shiite Spiritual Life
passage-en-01907

“They are the Perfect Divine Words (Kalimât tammât), which have neither a beginning nor any possibility of passing away. They are known by many different names, depending on the many different ways of looking at them: the Words of God (Kalimât Allah), the World of the Divine Command ('âlam al-Amr), the Keys to the Divine Mystery (Mafâtîh al-ghayb). They are the Witnesses of God and of His existence. ‘There is nothing whose treasuries are not with Us’ (2:21).”
VII. What the Imam Means in Shiite Spiritual Life
passage-en-01908

To call these “Perfect Words”—these Intelligences or beings of pure light—the Keepers of the treasure is also to say that they are the Treasures of divine knowledge. That is the identity expressed in the Imam's words.
VII. What the Imam Means in Shiite Spiritual Life
passage-en-01909

From two different points of view, they are at once Keepers and Treasures. Their difference and their identity are the same, Mulla Sadra observes, as in the cases we have already considered: the person who understands and the act of understanding; the sage and wisdom. “This is true of every attribute of an essence that exists only through the existence of the essence to which it belongs.”
VII. What the Imam Means in Shiite Spiritual Life
passage-en-01910

On the other hand—and this is where the highest point of his teaching about the Imam was coming into view—the hadith he is explaining gives the Imams themselves the title “Treasures and Keepers of the treasure of divine knowledge.” Everything just said about the cherubic Intelligences as “Perfect Words” must therefore apply, in one way or another, to the Imams as well.
